newsitem.title: UK: Stg weathers early wobble and warms to Labour govt.
newsitem.headline: Stg weathers early wobble and warms to Labour govt.

text.p: The British pound recovered all early losses made on news of a landslide election victory for the UK Labour Party and it ended the day in buoyant mood close to pre-election levels.

Analysts said the first Labour government in 18 years had been well discounted in advance. Few saw any significant change in economic policy and the prospect of a rise in UK interest rates as early as next week remains a bulwark for the currency.

"The sheer size of the Labour majority caused some initial jitters but the market has been collecting its thoughts since, and we think sterling is a buy from here," said Michael Burke, economist at U.S. firm Citibank. "All the uncertainty is now gone and rates are going up again."

Burke said he expected Labour's candidate for finance minister, Gordon Brown, to instruct the Bank of England to raise interest rates by at least a quarter of a percentage point when he meets central bank governor Eddie George on Wednesday.
The prospect of higher British interest rates after the election has been the engine behind sterling's relentless rally to 4-1/2-year highs. UK base lending rates are now 6.0 percent.
Brown said a Labour government would deliver its first budget within two months and would set monetary policy to meet the existing inflation target at 2.5 percent.
"We fully intend to keep all our promises and will move very quickly on a budget," he told ITN television news.
At 1400 GMT, the pound was at 2.7960/70 marks, little changed 2.7970/80 before the election results began trickling out late Thursday and up from from 2.7935/45 at the close here on Thursday.
The pound was at $1.6170/80 down slightly against a robust dollar from $1.6253/60 before the results and $1.6236/42 at the European close on Thursday.
The pound initially dipped to 2.7560 marks and about $1.6000 overnight as signs of an unexpectedly large Labour parliamentary majority, now estimated at 179 seats, unnerved traders in the Far East.
Analysts said there was some concern the size of the majority may allow a Labour government to drift back toward its more traditional policies of higher spending and taxation.
"Sterling has been very strong going into the election, and the big Labour victory will give policy-makers a free hand," said Tony Norfield, treasury economist at ABN Amro in London.
But others said a tight majority would have been an even greater risk because it could have left the survival of a new government up to a small band of left-wing Labour members.

"From a market perspective, the outcome is better than a narrow majority but sterling is broadly neutral on this result," said Joe Prendergast, foreign exchange strategist at Merrill Lynch. "Equally there is no fresh good news from this well discounted Labour victory and our medium-term forecasts remain the same."

Traders said much of the early wobble was a result of profit-taking by investors who had already been "long" of sterling going into the election. They said this was exaggerateed by an editorial opinion article in The Times newspaper urging Labour to allow the pound to weaken and tighten fiscal policy instead.
